sources.locator: "Battle of Ayacucho", revision 1375770122, § Background and § Aftermath

explanation: Junín is the stage of Bolívar's 1824 campaign that Ayacucho concluded. The Ayacucho article puts the two in one sequence: Bolívar "took advantage of the dismantling of the royalist defences and 'moved the whole month of May to Jauja', to face José de Canterac, who was isolated in Junín on 6 August 1824. Unrelenting prosecution of the war began, and 2700 royalists deserted and went over to the independentists. On 7 October 1824, with his troops before the gates of Cusco, Bolívar gave General Sucre command of the new battlefront" — the front on which Ayacucho was fought that December. The same article records how the victory was remembered: the Upper Peruvian independence act was dated 6 August 1825 "in honor of the Battle of Junín won by Bolivar". Probable, and a precondition rather than a cause: the article gives Junín as a step in the campaign, not as the reason Ayacucho was won.
